title: Environment Agency and Natural England face axe in Labour quango cull
summary:
Louise Haigh says the two environmental regulators are being reviewed as part of shake-up of arm’s length bodies

Ministers are considering abolishing two of England’s biggest environmental…

blocks.text: Ministers are considering abolishing two of England’s biggest environmental regulators in an attempt to give politicians greater control over what gets built and where.
Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, said on Monday that the Environment Agency and Natural England were being reviewed as part of a wider shake-up of arm’s length bodies.

Successive governments have argued that reforming or scrapping large environmental watchdogs would help free companies to build more houses and infrastructure. Environmentalists, however, warn such a move would endanger wildlife and would do little to boost growth.

Haigh told the CBI conference on Monday: “Over decades, politicians were content to duck accountability by giving responsibility away from ministers to a sprawling web of regulators and arm’s length bodies, more than 20 statutory consultees, all with veto power, notionally bound by statutory deadlines. But obfuscation has become normal.”

blocks.caption: Louise Haigh speaking at the CBI conference on Monday. Photograph: Neil Hall/EPA

blocks.text: She added: “As part of rewiring the state, we will reform arm’s length bodies to increase public control. We will look at each of their functions and pose the challenge: what should be devolved, what can be dissolved and what can be delivered by departments?
“We’ve already begun that process with the Environment Agency, Natural England, Ofwat and the Drinking Water Inspectorate.”

Ministers in successive governments have taken aim at both the Environment Agency and Natural England for blocking housebuilding in particular. The former prime minister Rishi Sunak wrote this weekend in the Sunday Times: “Natural England was able, without explicit parliamentary consent, to issue planning advice which held back the construction of 100,000 homes.”

Many of those frustrations were shared by the former chancellor Rachel Reeves, who blamed environmental regulators for choking economic growth by demanding developers build expensive wildlife protections such as the £100m “bat tunnel” over the HS2 high-speed rail line.

She told Sky News on Monday morning: “We’ve had successive governments complain about this, but unfortunately, successive governments have created more of these and pushed more decision-making out of their own departments, so that then when they make decisions they don’t agree with, they turn around and look in horror.”

Many of the proposals are likely to follow the recommendations made in a report by Jon Cunliffe last year, who proposed replacing Ofwat with a new super-regulator that would take in powers from Natural England and the Environment Agency.
Last month, the Conservatives announced that if they won power they would abolish both agencies, saying this would help create more new homes.

blocks.caption: The HS2 ‘bat tunnel’ in Buckinghamshire. Photograph: Jill Mead/The Guardian

blocks.text: The proposals have angered many in the environmental world. Tony Juniper, the chair of Natural England, said his organisation had helped speed up building by reviewing rules such as those that protect bats and newts.

Supporters say Natural England and the Environment Agency enforce legal duties that would still have to be enforced even if they did not exist. “A healthy natural environment is vital for economic development and at Natural England we are very proud of all the work we have done during recent years to unite our national ambitions for growth while achieving nature’s recovery,” Juniper said.
“It’s never been the case that healthy nature is in opposition to economic development, but actually enables it. It’s possible to do both.”

Craig Bennett, the chief executive of the Wildlife Trusts charity, said: “For over 16 years, politicians have been claiming that the regulations and regulators who protect English wildlife are some sort of obstacle on a path to prosperity. They are not. For over 16 years, protections have been chipped away and the woods, meadows, skylarks and hares they protect are suffering a death by a thousand cuts.”
Haigh said the review of quangos would be announced as part of next month’s 10-year plan, alongside further detail of how the government intends to bring utilities into public control.

She told her business-dominated audience it should not fear public control of companies currently in the private sector, saying it would help bring long-term certainty for investors. “We’ve built a hulking, complex behemoth of a regulatory state. It satisfies no one – not consumers, not investors. That is why public control should not alarm anyone in this room. It’s not ideological. It’s pragmatic, and it’s essential for people, for places, and for business.”
